Today's big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire?

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as President and CEO on Monday, Nov 23. He had resigned on Thursday, Nov 12. He was out for 11 days, which covered 7 trading sessions. Nvidia stock rose 31.5% on Monday.

Yes, this moved your S&P 500 fund, even if you never picked Nvidia. $1 million in VOO, the Vanguard S&P 500 fund, gained $44,639 on Monday alone. Measured with SPY, another S&P 500 fund, the lead over an equal-weight fund was bigger on only four of 5,929 trading days since May 2003.

The full round trip matters more than Monday. $1 million in VOO at the Nov 11 close was worth $950,684 at the Nov 23 close, price only. The same sum in an equal-weight fund was worth $955,850. The fund tilted to the biggest stocks lost more on the way down, and its bigger Monday bounce did not make up the difference.

How much did each fund move?

Most S&P 500 funds weight each stock by its market value, the share price times the shares. So the biggest companies move the fund most. RSP, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight fund, holds every stock in the same amount instead.

Nvidia fell 27.7% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 20 close. Over those days, $1 million in VOO shrank to $910,059. In RSP it shrank less, to $931,687.

Nvidia's slide pulled VOO down 9% in seven sessions, even for owners who never picked Nvidia. If that money has to pay your bills, a fall like that can push you to sell near the bottom. QQQ, a fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100, fell harder. $1 million in it was worth $881,326 at the Nov 20 close. Then it gained $69,981 on Monday. RSP gained $25,935 on the same $1 million.

QQQ opened 8% above Friday's close, its biggest opening jump ever, after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and its shares surged 31%.

Buyers at the open paid near the session high, and QQQ closed lower, so QQQM or QQEW suit holders wary of single-stock swings.

Every earlier record gap came during the dot-com bear market, so the jump offers only a weak sign that risk has passed.

Released: The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

If you bought the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) at the 9:30 a.m. ET bell on November 23, 2026, you paid $655.98 a share. By the close, that share was worth $651.03.

Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

That small loss came inside one of the strongest sessions in the fund's history. QQQ opened 7.81% above Friday's $608.45 close. That was its largest opening jump since trading began on March 10, 1999.

The move followed Monday, November 23 news from Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA): Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Shares rose 31.48% and added about $950 billion in market value.

What a Record Opening Gap Measures

An opening gap compares the day's first trade with the prior session's close. Monday's jump exceeded the previous record of 6.91%, set on December 8, 2000, which had edged out spreads of 6.01% on June 2, 2000 and 5.99% on April 18, 2001.

The fund's 7.00% close-to-close gain is large, but it falls short of a record. QQQ has posted 23 bigger daily gains, led by roughly 17% on January 3, 2001. The most recent was about 12% on April 9, 2025.

Buyers at the bell paid close to the $657.50 session high, then saw the fund drop as low as $641.95. Buying after a gap means paying for news that was already priced in before the first trade.

title: Pre-Markets Seeking Post-NVIDIA Equilibrium
detail:
Pre-Markets Seeking Post-NVIDIA Equilibrium
Mark Vickery
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 9:26 AM EST 4 min read
NVDA
QQQ
SPY
DIA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tuesday, November 24th, 2026

Pre-market futures are still trying to find their equilibrium after a breakneck past several trading days. After the NVIDIA NVDA saga began as a sad tale where its board felt the need to oust its CEO and seek a new way forward, and as of 24 hours ago snapped the CEO back in place as if nothing had happened, trading volume has gone nuts and the VIX has spiked to levels not seen in a long time.

At the core of this chain of events was the theft/clandestine sale of high-end AI chips to China. While the re-ascension of NVIDIA co-founder Jensen Huang to CEO on the one hand papers over this occurrence, on the other the U.S. is prepared to levy new tariffs on exports to China, and to a lesser degree other countries in Asia and Europe. The goods involved will mostly be of the heavy goods variety, like steel and autos, and not semiconductors used in AI.

In any case, markets are battling just north of break-even trading levels year to date, despite all major indexes having struck new all-time highs at some point within the year. (For the Nasdaq and S&P 500, these came as recently as early October; for the Dow and small-cap Russell 2000, these highs happened this past summer.) Normally Q4 is a time to sit back and watch funds accumulate from a year's worth of improving economic conditions; these days there are far too many questions currently unanswered.

We're quite unlikely to have heard the last of this series of events, either. Early January, a new U.S. Congress will be seated, and the Democrats who won big majorities in both houses are likely sharpening their knives in preparation for some major investigations, including into the NVIDIA matter(s), as surely as dinner tables across America are preparing to carve up Thanksgiving turkey. So the questions look to be with us through the end of the year.

Case-Shiller September Numbers Remain Steady

A half-hour ahead of today's open, the Case-Shiller Home Price Index for September (typically a couple months in arrears) has been released, keeping steady at +2.1%, precisely where the August headline reported. Considering year-over-year inflation is likely between 3.7-4.0%, we see that housing prices are still not keeping up with inflation. This has been the case for 16 consecutive months now.

Chicago has now led in price increases for the 20-city survey for the seventh-straight month, accelerating to +6.9% in September. The Windy City is followed by New York (+5.8%) and Miami, FL (+4.6%). The three cities posting negative housing growth for the month are again Denver, Dallas, and bottom of the list Seattle (-1.9%). A quick look back to five years ago showed Seattle among the top U.S. cities in home price increases.

Here's Why Investors Should Go Defensive Now: ETFs in Focus

Wall Street was in the red last week. The Nasdaq Composite plunged as much as 10%, the S&P 500 retreated about 8.6%, the Dow Jones fell about 8.1%. The S&P 500 and the Dow closed in correction while the Nasdaq 100 just had its worst week since March 2020.

State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust SPY is about 1% so far this year (as of Nov. 22, 2026). State Street SPDR Dow Jones Indust Avg ETF Trust DIA has retreated about 0.5% and the Nasdaq-100 ETF Invesco QQQ Trust, Series 1 QQQ is off about 0.8%.

The S&P 500's decisive break below its 200-day moving average triggered selling by trend-following investors. Traders often tend to sell when markets breach key technical levels, further creating downward pressure.

U.S. Companies Shift From Buybacks to Share Sales

U.S. companies are increasingly issuing new shares instead of buying back their own stock, adding to the supply that the four-year bull market must absorb. This shift could create another hurdle for stocks after years of strong gains, as quoted on CNBC.

Acadian Asset Management's analysis shows that net new share issuance reached 3.1% of total market capitalization by late last week (per CNBC). Several major companies have recently turned to equity markets to raise capital. These companies include the likes of Oracle, Meta, SpaceX and Alphabet.

Equity Issuance Often Signals Market Caution

A 2000 study by Malcolm Baker and Jeffrey Wurgler found that periods of heavy equity issuance relative to debt issuance were often followed by weaker stock market returns. The findings suggested that corporate managers tend to issue shares when they believe market valuations are attractive, per the above-mentioned CNBC article.

The Baker-Wurgler equity share, which measures equity issuance as a proportion of total stock and bond issuance, peaked at around 18% in 2021. It has climbed again in recent months, although it remains below that high.

Sticky Inflation

The Iran conflict has pushed oil above $83 a barrel, while Strait of Hormuz transit fees keep pressure on prices. Persistent inflation has raised expectations of further Fed rate hikes, with officials warning of a potentially more aggressive tightening path.

Treasury yields surged above 5% before easing on safe-haven buying. Meanwhile, reports that the Trump administration may resume strikes on Iran have added to geopolitical uncertainty.

At the time of writing, there are 96.2% chances of a quarter basis point rate hike in December, up from 68.9% probability, a month ago, per CME FedWatch Tool.
